name: erlang@27
desc: Programming language for highly scalable real-time systems
why: Erlang's actor model and hot code loading are strange and worth a look, though it is a mainstream runtime.

brief.what_it_is: Erlang is a programming language, with its runtime and the OTP library and tooling set, for building massively scalable soft real-time systems that need high availability. Its runtime has built-in support for concurrency, distribution and fault tolerance. You write functional code with pattern matching and recursion, run it in an interactive shell, and spawn lightweight processes that communicate by sending and receiving messages. OTP adds libraries, design principles, a distributed database, cross-language interfaces, and debugging and release-handling tools. The package installed here, erlang@27, is the OTP 27 line; the homepage is pitched at OTP 29.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage describes Erlang as used in telecoms, banking, e-commerce, computer telephony and instant messaging, where systems must stay up and handle huge numbers of concurrent activities. Its framing is practical functional programming for a parallel world.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage's examples show lightweight processes created with spawn, with messages passed using ! and received with receive. One example runs a parallel map-reduce by spawning a process per number and collecting replies. The page does not explain the runtime internals.

commands_seen.context: Erlang shell input from the homepage, calling a factorial function defined in a module called example; prints 3628800.
Erlang shell input from the homepage that sends the atom go to a spawned child process.
Downloads page: the one-line source build for a pre-built archive, per the page's 'in a nutshell' description.
Downloads page: Homebrew line for macOS, listed among the pre-built package managers.
Downloads page: package line for Ubuntu and Debian.
Downloads page: Docker line for running Erlang in a container.

brief.install_notes: The downloads page offers a source build (./configure && make && make install), a Windows 64-bit installer and zip archive, and HTML/PDF docs and man pages. It also points to third-party version managers kerl, asdf and mise, and to setup-beam for GitHub Actions. The page says OS package managers can lag behind the latest release, so a specific version may require building from source. Nothing on these pages mentions accounts or runtime prerequisites beyond the build tools needed to compile from source.
brief.standout: Erlang's concurrency model is the unusual part: lightweight processes that share nothing and communicate only through messages, which the homepage demonstrates in a few lines of shell. The OTP layer is what turns the language into a system-building toolkit for fault-tolerant services.
brief.status: Maintained. The homepage lists a news item for Erlang/OTP 29.1 dated September 16, 2026, described as the first maintenance patch for OTP 29, and the downloads page gives 29.1.2 as the latest version. Commits and issue activity were not checked.
brief.caveats: The homepage is marketing-oriented, so I did not get deep technical documentation. Since OTP 18.0 it is Apache License 2.0; older releases were under the Erlang Public License. The homepage frames it as soft real-time, not hard real-time. The Homebrew package is versioned erlang@27, which is an older line than the 29.x releases the site promotes. The scout note mentions hot code loading, but I did not see it on the pages I read.

OTP is set of Erlang libraries and design principles providing middle-ware to develop these systems.

judge.reason: Erlang’s isolated message-passing processes and OTP fault-tolerance model make a distinctive, still-relevant system-building language most developers haven’t explored.

entry.title: Erlang/OTP 27
entry.tldr: A functional language and runtime built around tiny isolated processes that talk by message, made for systems that must keep running.
entry.deeper_look:
Erlang is a programming language, its runtime, and OTP, a set of libraries and design principles for building services. The runtime has concurrency, distribution and fault tolerance built in. You write functional code with pattern matching and recursion, try it in an interactive shell, and spawn lightweight processes that share nothing and communicate only by sending and receiving messages.

The homepage says it is used in telecoms, banking, e-commerce, computer telephony and instant messaging, places where systems must stay up while handling huge numbers of concurrent activities. Its own line is "Practical functional programming for a parallel world". It describes the target as soft real-time, not hard real-time.

The idea underneath is that concurrency is the basic building block, not a library bolted on. On the homepage, a child process is created with spawn, sent a message with `Child ! go`, and handles it in a receive block. One example runs a parallel map-reduce by spawning a process per number and collecting the replies. OTP then builds on that with tooling for releases, debugging, and a distributed database.

This formula is the OTP 27 line. The homepage is pitched at OTP 29, so this is an older release series, which is fine for poking at the language but not the newest.
entry.install:
brew install erlang@27
# Man pages: erl -man, or add $HOMEBREW_PREFIX/opt/erlang@27/lib/erlang/man to MANPATH.
# Pulls in openssl, unixodbc and wxwidgets as dependencies.

try_this.what_happens: Starts the interactive Erlang shell, where you can type expressions and define and run code.
In the shell, calls a factorial function from the homepage's example module and prints 3628800. You need to compile that module first.
Sends the atom go as a message to a spawned child process, as in the homepage's process example.

entry.whats_unique: Isolated lightweight processes that only exchange messages are the core of the language, not an add-on. OTP turns that into a toolkit for building fault-tolerant services.
entry.caveats: This package is the older OTP 27 line while the site promotes 29.x, and the homepage is marketing-oriented, so expect to find deeper documentation elsewhere.
